chunks: Muhammad ibn al-Hasan and my father - may God be pleased with them - narrated that Sa'd ibn Abdullah narrated from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn ibn Abi al-Khattab, from al-Hakam ibn Maskin al-Thaqafi, from Sulayman ibn Zarif, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

I asked him: 'May I be your ransom, why do we testify that those who oppose us are disbelievers and [will go to] the Fire, but we do not testify for ourselves and our companions that they are in Paradise?' He said: 'That is due to your weakness. If there are no major sins among you, then testify that you are in Paradise.' I asked: 'And what are the major sins, may I be your ransom?' He said: 'The greatest of the major sins is associating partners [with God], disobedience to parents, becoming a foreigner after migration, accusing a chaste woman [of adultery], fleeing from the ranks [in battle], devouring the property of an orphan unjustly, usury after clear proof [of its prohibition], and killing a believer.' I said to him: 'What about adultery and theft?' He said: 'They are not like those [major sins].'

The compiler of this book - may God be pleased with him - said: 'The narrations regarding the major sins are not contradictory, although some mention five, some seven, some eight, and some more. For every sin after shirk is great in comparison to what is smaller than it, and every small sin is great in comparison to what is smaller than it, and every great sin is small in comparison to shirk with God the Exalted.'

key_terms.أَكْلُ مَالِ الْيَتِيمِ ظُلْمًا: Devouring the property of an orphan unjustly
key_terms.قَذْفُ الْمُحْصَنَةِ: Accusing a chaste woman of adultery

ai.seo_question: What are the major sins in Shia Islam and how does the Imam define their hierarchy?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Saduq highlights the Imam’s nuanced view that believers' hesitation stems from spiritual humility rather than certainty of damnation, listing key major sins like shirk, disobedience to parents, and fleeing battle. The compiler clarifies that variations in the count of major sins across narrations are not contradictory, as sin magnitude is relative, with shirk remaining the ultimate benchmark. This reflects the Shia scholarly tradition of balancing textual specificity with theological flexibility in understanding divine justice.
